subtopic: REDISTRIBUTION
speechtext: I beg to put to the Government a question of which I gave notice, as to whether they proposed bringing down, at this session, a measure providing for redistribution.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REDISTRIBUTION
speechtext: The Government has no desire to delay the bringing down of such a measure, but the Government does not wish to proceed with undue haste in the matter. As my right hon. friend knows, a measure of redistribution is one that is likely to occupy a considerable share of the time of the House, both in committee and in subsequent discussion in the chamber; and as it is not anticipated that there is any desire for a general election between now and the end of the year, the Government has felt that redistribution might well stand until the next session of Parliament.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
There was a good deal of discussion the other day on this clause, which relates to the inclusion of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. There was, of course, a difference of opinion as to whether this force should be included or not. Almost every member of the House had a good word to say for the force, but they differed somewhat on the advisability of maintaining the force at its full strength. There seemed to be a general consensus of opinion that perhaps it would not be wise to include in the Defence Department the control of the mounted police, the argument being that this force was created as a civil and not a military force and should remain such. I do not feel like combatting that view to any extent, as undoubtedly the facts stated are correct. This much, however, the committee will bear in mind, that, in taking this step, we shall be unable to carry on the economies that were expected to be effected by the combination of executive staffs of these two branches. As was stated the other afternoon, it was thought that the civil staff of the mounted police could, in a large measure, outside of temporary employees, be worked into the new department without hardship to any person and with increased efficiency of the combined
National Defence

Department of Defence. If we accept the proposal that the police branch be not attached to the Department of Defence, we shall not be able to do that. I think it is fair to say to the committee-I forgot to mention this the other afternoon-[DOT] that for the last couple of months the Minister of Militia has been administering the Mounted Police. It was in the Justice Department when the Government came into power, and it was transferred or attached to the outside, without giving authority to the minister.
I believe it is the opinion of the committee generally that the Mounted Police might be greatly reduced in numbers. Of course, if we intend to restrict the activities of the force to the unorganized territories the force will be very small. There will always be work in connection with the Mounted Police in the city of Ottawa and vicinity. I would not say that the work of the force ought to be restricted altogether to the unorganized territories. I have communicated with the several provincial premiers, and while I have not heard from all, the correspondence that I have so far received leads me to think that perhaps it would not be wise, all at once, to withdraw all the forces from the provinces. As our Object is not so much to stand on technical differences as to protect the people where we can, I want the committee to consider what the various premiers have said. I will not encumber Hansard' with al the letters but will give a synopsis of the reply from each province. Ontario thinks that the Canadian Mounted Police would be of material assistance in the enforcement of law and order if proper co-operation between the Dominion and the province could be established. The Prime Minister of Quebec thinks that some use might be made of the Mounted Polite in Ungava and the northern portions of that province, but so far as the older and settled parts are concerned he does not think that it is wise to continue their services.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The province of Nova Scotia thinks that some advantage might be gained if it. .were able to call upon a federal police at any time. As regards Saskatchewan, Premier Martin thinks that some arrangement should be made such as existed prior to 1917, by which the Mounted Police should have charge of the enforcement of criminal law. The province of New Brunswick was somewhat canny; it has not so far replied. Its premier

thinks that the maintenance of a force there might cost the province something, and the matter has not yet been decided because it would depend on the services that could be rendered. In some cases it might be well to ask the provinces assisted to help in some of the expense. No replies have been received from British Columbia, Manitoba, Alberta and Prince Edward Island. Under the present circumstances I think it is impossible for us to come to any fast and firm decision as to what we should do, but I take it as the view of the committee that, whether or not the Mounted Police be included in the new Defence Department, the number of men in that force could be materially reduced. As I pointed out, I do not strongly hold the view that it ought to be brought info the Department of Defence, for the reason adduced by hon. gentlemen, that it is a civil force; and as the estimated economy to be effected by the amalgamation of the two executives cannot be expected1 if the police be not taken absolutely into the Defence Department, it will not make any material difference as to the authority of the Government to reduce the police force to any size it may think .wise. To meet the wishes of the committee I move that in line 3 of the section the words "Air and Police" be struck out and the words "and Air" be substituted therefor.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I highly commend the minister for his decision. It is true, it robs the bill of about its only radical feature, but it is a wise move to leave the Mounted Police out. The Police, as has been stated, is a civil force. I do not see, however, that the minister's point, that he is going to be disarmed from effecting economies, has any force. If the Mounted Police are left in the Militia, then the officers of that department will be in control of the force. As minister of that department my hon. friend will be requisitioned for the services of the Mounted Police, and gradually in the public mind the opinion will grow that the force are a part of the military organization of Canada. Now, they are no part of the defence of the country; they are a part of the force for the maintenance of law and order, which is not a function of the Militia or the Defence Department. It is far more a function of the Justice Department, and previously the Dominion Police were under that department. When the Mounted Police came in they remained under that department for a time, and then both went under the department

National Defence
that had controlled the Mounted Police before. While the Department of Justice is not responsible for the maintenance of law and order, nevertheless its functions are closely related thereto, and by placing the police under that department and utilizing its officers, economy can be effected in that way, just as well as in the Militia Department, if it is really desired to eliminate high-paid officers. I was glad to hear the minister's remarks about the reduction of the Mounted Police. I do not doubt that a reduction could now be effected; but if I measure the opinion of the minister aright it does not differ very much from my own, that anything in the nature of reckless or wanton reduction now would be very poor economy, and instead of meeting public opinion would go in defiance thereof. I hope the force will be reduced to the utmost extent possible, consistent with serving the purposes of the Mounted Police, but no further. The minister in his communications with the premiers of the provinces has so far received the replies which I should have expected. I do not like to prophesy, but I think that when he hears from the other premiers in the West they will give very much the same judgment as that of the premier of Saskatchewan. By the way, I observed applause when the minister stated that the police would not be required in the older parts of the province of Quebec, but might be used in the district of IJngava. Why the distinction? If the maintenance of law and order is wholly a provincial function, and if we are not justified in assuming any part of it, we have no more right to go into Ungava than into the older parts of Quebec. They might be able to use the police more in Ungava, it is true, but the principle of the division of constitutional jurisdiction applies just as much to Ungava as to the city of Montreal. It is a question of expense, that is all; and the force may be needed as much in Quebec as in any other province. If we are to maintain a fluid reserve force for the purposes for which the police are established, it is hard to justify saying to three, or four or five provinces: "We will maintain a force at your disposal, subject to your requisition," and to three or four other provinces:	"The force
shall not be subject to your requisition at all." I do not know how that stand could be justified, and consequently the minister's present state of mind is about the right one [DOT]-to reduce where he can. We are getting further from war conditions and some reduction may be possible, but the main purpose of the Mounted Police will not permit of any wanton or reckless reduction of the force, or the contraction of its utility from the purpose which it is now constituted to fulfil.

speechtext: Is it intended that the official here referred to shall receive, in addition to the salary of a deputy head of a department, extra remuneration as a member of the Defence Council?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Not at all. The Naval Service is peculiar in itself, as those who have administered that department know, and, for the present at least, the Government is desirous of retaining the services of the present Deputy Minister of the Naval Service, who understands the work of that department better than any one else, even the Deputy Minister of the Defence Department. In the Naval Service Department there are many technical branches, such as hydrographic surveys, radiotelegraphic service, and that kind of thing. I take the House into my confidence and say I want the authority to retain Mr. Desbarats, the present occupant of the office, as deputy to manage that part of the service, for a time, at least. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: His salary as deputy is $6,000 a year?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
If you are going to have two deputy heads you will ,not accomplish what the bill sets out to attain. It is true that there are many branches of the Naval Service Department, but when they are all added together, the department is really an exceeding^ small one. The
proposal here is merely to change the title of the Deputy Minister of the Naval Service and take him into the Defence Council. He will get the same salary; he will rank as deputy head; to all intents and purposes he will occupy the same position ,that he occupies to-day. That is not an amalgamation at all. The late government brought together the Inland Revenue and the Customs Departments. In each of these departments there had been a deputy minister, but we let one go and brought the two services together under a single deputy head. I am satisfied that there is in the Department of Militia a deputy minister who can take care of the whole amalgamated service-a man of long experience, of great intelligence and capacity for work. It looks to me as if this proposal was put forth merely for the purpose of including somebody whom the Government did not want to displace and to continue him in the same rank and at the same salary. I would like to know more of the reasons for retaining Mr. Desbarats, or anybody else, in the rank of deputy head. The work can all be done by a single deputy minister. You can save $6,000 a year by striking out this subsection; I certainly am opposed to it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: A few days ago I commended the minister for his efforts in bringing these departments together, his aim being, as I believed, to bring about greater efficiency and economy. But I cannot see where the economy will come in so far as this particular appointment goes. In bringing the two departments .together there should be only one deputy minister. Of course, there would be at the head of the military branch the Chief of the General Staff, and at the head of the naval branch a technical officer whose advice could be sought in matters pertaining to that part of the service. But if the two departments are to be merged to have only one deputy head will result in greater economy and efficiency.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE

Yesterday my hon.
friends were warning me very strongly against depriving any official of his position; they seem to have changed their attitude since then.

Naval Service under their jurisdiction, so I warn the committee-

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Well, that was temporary. No one has a higher opinion of the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence than I have. Whom will that staff
be under as a deputy head?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That will be by agreement, but largely, if not altogether, I think, under the Deputy Minister of the Defence Department. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
That is practically the
organization we have now. We have a Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries now, Mr. Johnston, a Deputy Minister of Naval Service, Mr. Desbarats, and a Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, Sir Eugene Fiset; and the only change you propose is to take the Naval Service into the other department under the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, retaining the Deputy Minister of the Naval Service, Mr. Desbarats, but calling him something else. That is not a consolidation or amalgamation, to my way of thinking. I feel sure

that you could drop Mr. Desbarats and carry out your scheme without him, saving the country $6,000 per annum. You would depend then for your guidance in regard to matters pertaining to the Naval Service upon an expert in that department. By the present scheme you are just continuing another deputy head, without giving him that name, saving the position perhaps for-what shall I say?-a friend, political or otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It makes a difference to my hon. friend, I suppose, who is being hit.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
It is not simply a
matter of saving $6,000, but once you retain the deputy head of that department, he is going to concentrate his energies upon holding the whole department. He will consider every time he gives up a man that he has made a surrender to the other deputy, and the other deputy in turn will consider that everything he does in the way of compromise is a surrender. In a word, the minister is maintaining an organization that will prevent him from accomplishing anything in the way of the object he has in mind. Perhaps not wholly prevent him, but it will prevent him to such an extent that he will never get very far. He is putting obstacles in his own way that he will find it very difficult to surmount. Why could not the same thing be done in this case as was done when the Inland Revenue Department was amalgamated with the Customs Department? Where are the different circumstances? The Inland Revenue Department had been wholly distinct from the Customs; the officers were distinct; the deputy head was distinct; the work was wholly distinct, just as distinct in every particular as is the work of the Naval Service from the work of the Militia Department to-day. But we let go Mr. Vincent, the Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue, and placed the two departments under the Deputy Minister of Customs. It is true we were not at all harsh with Mr. Vincent. He got a year's salary, 4 p.m. perhaps a little more, and I would have no objection to Mr. Desbarats being treated the same. But when you maintain the deputy head, you maintain the department, and there is no consolidation; you may call it consolidation, but it is not consolidation at all. The minister in the first ten minutes this afternoon, wisely, I think, dropped about half of this bill. If he insists on holding this clause, I^think he is dropping the other half.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I do not think the minister should assume that attitude. I am not approaching this matter with any desire to destroy the value of the minister's effort. speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I only rise to point out to the House that this is the first time I have ever heard of Mr. Desbarats being anything but capable and courteous. I know him well; I have known him for years before I came here. Sometimes of course in our enthusiasm even a member of the House will ask a deputy for things which he ought to ask from the minister, because the minister only has authority to do these things; some of them a deputy should not do. My hon. friend suggested, rather sneeringly, that I should give this matter consideration.	I can assure him
that I have given it consideration every day for the last six weeks, and I think I can arrive at a conclusion that will satisfy myself after six weeks study of a matter that he can dispose of in half an hour. I want to give the committee all the information possible.	My judgment and
the judgment of the Government, after fully considering this question of retaining the Deputy Minister of the Naval Service, is that the only satisfactory way, under the conditions, to bring about this amalgamation, which must come about gradually and cannot be the work of a moment, is that the able deputy minister should be retained for the time being in his present position as head of the Naval Service branch..

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
It does not seem to me that any very serious objection can be taken to the proposal of the minister in this respect. I have no desire to enter
National Defence

into any discussion of the merits or demerits of Mr. Desbarats. I have always understood he was a highly efficient officer, but, as I understand it, what the minister is proposing is that the services of Mr. Desbarats may be available for a period until the organization is complete, and he has given some reasons for that course. The clause authorizes the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the minister, to appoint this officer. It is merely a permissive authority. I quite agree that a good deal of exception might be taken to having a department with two gentlemen in the capacity of deputy ministers, and I am not going to discuss the merits or demerits of Major General Fiset. As far as I know, these gentlemen are both very capable men. It seems to me, however, that we should give some latitude to the minister in carrying on the reorganization, and my hon. friends to my right are scarcely quite consistent in the position they have taken on this question; because, if I recall aright, when this matter was first under consideration a few days ago, both my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) who was the Minister of Militia in the late government, and his predecessor, my hon. friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn), took the position quite strongly that officers in the Militia Department should be looked after. I believe that latitude should be given to the minister to carry on this re-organization in the way he thinks best for the service. If there are two deputy ministers next year, or the following year, and this Parliament is asked to vote their salaries, the question then can very well come up for reconsideration. We are not passing legislation that will put this matter away beyond our control. The principle is sound, and once the principle -of a bill is sound -and I think the minister's explanations are fairly reasonable in respect to carrying it out-then I think he should give the minister the necessary latitude to carry it into effect.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I think, perhaps, nobody in this House or outside of it has criticised the Naval estimates more than I have. I am opposed to the present so-called Canadian navy, for the simple reason that it is no navy, and never will be any navy, and is only a waste of money. But I agree with the hon. gentleman from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) when he says the minister should be given a chance to re-organize his department, and should have the advice, for a short time, of the gentleman who has
TMr, Crerar.j
been deputy head of naval affairs. I do not see how the re-organization is going to take place, in view of the fact that we now have only one cruiser and two destroyers, to protect the Atlantic coast from the people who may come down from Greenland some night and destroy all our cities, or to protect the Pacific coast from some other enemy who may come from Alaska. And this cruiser and these two torpedo boats, I may say, have been hibernating in the West Indies for the last six months. I say we have no navy, and the quicker we get clear of these boats the better, and the quicker we clean up the $215,000 voted last year for overhead expenses in Ottawa, in regard to the navy, which would be voted this year, the better. I say that the Minister of Militia should have a chance to keep Mr. Desbarats for one or two years, until the mess is cleaned up. I cannot agree with the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) that Major General Fiset can do the work in connection with the Naval Department. Would the hon. gentleman say, if something happened Major General Fiset, and he resigned, that Mr. Desbarats could do his work in the Militia Department? Of course he could not. Neither could Major General Fiset, good a man as we all know he is, do the work which Mr. Desbarats does in regard to naval affairs. I say, certainly, let us have economy, not only in this department but in other departments, but for the present, much as I am opposed to the so-called Canadian navy, and much as I would like to see the whole thing wiped out, I agree with the hon. gentleman from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) that for the present Mr. Desbarats' services should be retained.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
As I understand the
proposal, it is not merely for the present time, or in the nature of a temporary proposal at all. The hon. gentleman from Marquette intimated that during the process of reorganization it would be well to retain Mr. Desbarats. This is a permanent arrangement, not for the process of reorganization at all. My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) says that it is necessary to retain the services of Mr. Desbarats for a year or two years, and let us do it. If that were his suggestion, it would alter the situation very much.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Could we not amend the
act next year?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
We can amend any act of this Parliament whenever we like, but

National Defence
we must go on the assumption that this is a permanent arrangement and not a temporary one. That is what the bill says, and it says nothing about a temporary arrangement, so that we must assume and presume that it is the ordinary permanent appointment. I draw a strong distinction between a person in the position of Mr. Desbarats and a person in the position of one of the higher offices of that department, to whom I referred a few days ago. I thought I made myself clear on that occasion; if not, I shall try to do so now or later on during the discussion of this bill. I say that we should retain as far as possible the services of those men who, through their ability and experience, and through gallantry in the field of action, have risen to high command and high military positions. That is a principle, I submit, that we should maintain.
Subsection 3 of section 5 agreed to.
On subsection 4-Controller:

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I ask the Minister of Militia, have they a purchasing commission connected with the department, or is it just one officer in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: We have a purchasing department, but it has no connection with the Purchasing Commission. I pointed that out the other night that two or three of the gentlemen in this department are doing the work of clerk. They were on the list of the Civil Service Commission. They were given the title of "assisting purchasing agent," and they are doing the work in the department. And this department, and all departments, whether they purchase through the Purchasing Commission or not, are responsible for their requisitions, and the details afterwards pass through the Purchasing Commission for confirmation.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: If I understand aright, the position of controller, to be created under this section, is largely that of a chief accountant or a paymaster-general or something of that kind. He is not a purchasing agent in any sense of the word. He is in the nature of a chief accountant in the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I tell the House frankly I have not seen the man, and have not appointed him at all, and possibly I may transfer some one in the department, but with my casual observation in a large department of this kind I think the financial end could be managed more successfully if they have a shrewd financial man to oversee all the expenditure of money in the
department particularly as the other branches also are being brought in. I was calling him "financial comptroller," and my object was to get a good, able business man, whom I could consult in connection with all expenditures of every branch of the department, a man who would be responsible to myself and the deputy head for every dollar expended.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Is this the creation
of a new position?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: How was the financial end of the department handled before?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: We have an accounting branch, an audit branch, and a paymaster's branch, and it maybe that I may take one of the men in charge of these branches. I admit I had in mind doing something else. If we were running a business of this magnitude as a private concern, we would have some man of the description I have given, and he could possibly save his salary in a month. If, in the department, there is a man of that capacity that I could appoint to this position, it would be my object to do so; but if I did not find such a man, I wanted to feel free to go into the business world to find one.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The minister is on
absolutely sound lines. I know, from my short experience while f was in charge of the Militia Department, there was sadly needed a capable business man to oversee the finances of the organization.
Sub-section 4 of section 5 agreed to.
On sub-section 5-holder of any position abolished' may be appointed to another position:

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Is there in the Militia Department a practice whereby a man who occupies a certain position under which the department should have all his time, is given some other work to do which he should do in his time, but for doing this work, he is given another salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I do not know of a case except that of a deputy minister in several departments, who have a combination of salaries. As to the ordinary civil servant, I do not know of a case. I have been asked that question several times in communications, and I asked my department to make investigation, but up to date, I have not found such a case.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Does the minister not
think it would be fair to the House and to
National Defence

the country to give a deputy minister a straight salary without giving him so much for this and so much for that? In that way, the people would know exactly what salary he was receiving.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The salary of my
deputy minister has been explained in this House several times. I shall be glad to explain it again, but I think the question is hardly germane to this discussion.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I hope the minister will not overlook the importance of retaining those high officials of the Militia Department, men like Sir Henry Burstall and Major-General MacBrien. It has cost a great deal to produce military experts like those men, and their services are necessary. While the principle of the bill, which is to effect co-ordination of and economy in the various branches of the service which have to do with the defence of the country, may be all right, I am of opinion that if these military experts were retained, perhaps in another sphere of activity under this clause of the bill, they could effelet a great deal of economy. I do not think the country expects very much curtailment in military expenditures; you may spend a great deal of the nation's money and not get very much for it. The question is not the amount of money which is spent, but how it is spent. I hope the minister will not overlook the fact that highly trained officials like these can save the country many millions of dollars, not only in the Department of Militia, but in other affairs. Officers whom I have consulted in No. 2 Military District, the Toronto District, are of the opinion that it is a retrograde step for the Militia Department to lose the services of these high experts , at such a critical stage in the ' history	of this
country, just after the war and begin everything over again. At such a time as this we need the services of these trained men and we should retain them. I feel that an economy will be effected by retaining their services, and I hope the minister will consider the suggestion which I have very humbly made.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Will the minister tell the committee which of the principal officers are likely to lose their positions in the service by reason of this amalgamation? In the papers we have seen that Major-General Sir Henry Burstall and Major-General Gwatkin are both to be allowed to retire. Are any of the other chief officers to be retired likewise?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I would not like to be held as making a pledge, because conditions might change, but there is no need for alarm. The suggestion of dispensing with the services of any of these officers has not been considered at all.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The point is simply
this that the minister is dispensing, or has dispensed, with the services of one of the most experienced and one of the highest in rank of the officers in Canada. I think the retirement of Major-General Sir Henry Burstall has already taken place officially. As I understand the matter, he is now out of the service, and so, I believe, is Major-General Gwatkin. In the case of the latter, the facts are not quite the same as they are in regard to Sir Henry Burstall. Major-General Gwatkin is a very able Imperial officer, who came to Canada shortly before or during the war, who has remained in Canada since and whose services were of the greatest value to Canada during the war. I understand that Major-General Gwatkin is entitled to an Imperial pension. At the conclusion of the war, he was virtually retired or retiring from the service, and his services were enlisted by the Canadian Air Board. For the past year and a half or two years he has been in charge of the Canadian Air Service, and it may well be, in his case, that retirement is proper. I know that he has no very great desire to continue in the service, and he rather helped us out in a situation which we had on hand a year or two ago. His services to Canada, however, have been of the highest. He is a very able and tried experienced officer, a man who made his mark in the Imperial service long before he came to Canada.
The case of Major-General Sir Henry Burstall is a litle different. That officer is a Canadian, a man now of military age, I believe only 51 or 52 years old, a man who joined the Canadian service as a provisional lieutenant away back in 1888 or 1889, a graduate of our Royal Military College, a Staff College man-for he went to England and took there, at the expense of this country the course which many of our leading officers have received. He there obtained that special and particular knowledge which is so hard to acquire, namely, the knowledge that is necessary for a staff officer. The hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) a day or two ago mentioned in the House that staff officers were, perhaps, not as highly appreciated by ordinary individuals as they

National Defence
should be. But there is no question about the fact that the greatest difficulty in time of trouble is to secure competent staff officers. It is not a hard thing to get an ordinary officer. He can be trained easily and without much loss of time. The staff is a very different thing. It requires a long course of training, and for that reason we in Canada for many years back have been accustomed to send a number of our most prominent and most promising officers to the Staff College at Cam-berley to take the necessary course. Only a few days ago General Sir Arthur Currie discussed the question with the newspapers in Montreal. He strongly objects to any proposal to retire Major General Sir Henry Burstall from the service. He points out that you cannot easily get men to fill positions like his. We want in the service men who have the qualifications and experience. We have trained such men and paid the expenses for that training, and these men, who have acquitted themselves well, have now the advantage of four or five years' experience of actual warfare. They are thoroughly competent and in every way equipped, by education and otherwise; and now because there is a re-organization of the Militia you let out one of the most effective and useful of officers. Is there not in this re-organization some place where a man like Sir Henry Burstall can be utilized? Can he not be put in charge of some necessary and suitable work in order that the valuable services of which he is capable may be retained? Surely hi3 experiences and his ability are worth a lot to the country. Why dispense with him? That is the point I want to have cleared up. I sincerely trust that all these officers on the headquarters staff who have had experience are going to be retained- The minister does not want to bind himself in respect of them, but here is a specific case where a man has already been retired. Again I ask, is it not possible in the Militia of this country to maintain the services of a man who has done such excellent work and acquitted himself so admirably, and who should be a very valuable officer in the department?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: As one of those who served at the front, I may say that General Burstall, who was a staff officer over there-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: He was more than a staff officer.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Yes, he was in charge of the Second Division, and I met him in
the lines on many occasions. There was no man I know who served over there, with the possible exception, of Sir Arthur Currie, who had a higher standing with the men of all ranks than General Burstall. I desire to do him that justice. I am aware that the minister himself spoke highly of him the other day, but it has been a puzzle to me,, since reading in the press that he is to be retired, with a pension, I believe, to understand, on what grounds he is being dispensed with. As the ex-Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) has said, no man in Canada has a better standing in military matters than General Burstall.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: If the stand taken by the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) were to be taken as a sound basis for the department to go upon, then I should think that care would have necessarily to be taken of every man who made a splendid record at the front in the war. I have no doubt that the gentleman in question not only made a splendid name for himself, but also enhanced the reputation of the Canadian soldiers. We must remember, however, that thousands of other men did exactly the same thing, though perhaps they did not all win so brilliant a name.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: But I have referred to men of the permanent force who in their boyhood agreed to serve the Government of Canada in that force, and have done so ever since. Now the Government is turning them out.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is now, of course, on safer ground. But we are coming to the time when we shall have to reduce the expenditures of the Militia Department, in common with all the other departments of Government, and it is essential that we make a beginning. And because a man has given the best in him to the service of the permanent force of Canada is, I submit, no reason why he should be retained if he is not required. Not only that, but an hon. member tells me that this gentleman is getting a pension, which I hope is a reasonable pension for one in his position. I do not think that that is an unreasonable ground to take in a matter of this kind. Personally, I hope that the time will soon come when we shall be able materially to reduce the burden of the Militia Department, and I trust that the minister in the next few years will be able to rid his department, always under fair and reasonable terms, of very many of those who are now employed in it, and
National Defence

who are not actually giving, in the present condition of the country, services commensurate with the salaries they are receiving.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I do not wish to
weary the House with any long quotations, hut I read a few days ago a speech made by General Sir Douglas Haig, who, as we know, was in command of the British army in France. In unveiling a memorial at Camberley Staff College, which I think is recognized as the greatest staff college in the world, General Haig said:
In the desire to retrench, and especially to economise on defence forces, there is a great danger that governments may go too far. The staff has always been a favorite target for those who do not understand either it or its functions.
Further on he says:
A nation industrially efficient and with a sound national character can improvise much in war, as our history in the war has shown; but principles are things that cannot readily be improvised. They have to be evolved by deep study and clear thinking through many years, tested often by the touchstone of experience. Our two staff colleges and the "p.s.c." officer gave us the sound military principles on which the war was fought and won.
He goes on to speak of the work of staff officers in France and also of the necessity for ensuring that future generations shall reap the benefit of their experience. I quote further:
Whatever a nation may do, it is a mistake to imagine that an army can muddle through a great war and reach victory at the end against an efficient and highly trained enemy. The handicap we started with from the smallness of our military forces could never have been overtaken if the pre-war training of our regular army, the military education of its officers, and its system of organization and command, had not been all on the right lines. It is no small consolation on such an occasion as this to feel and know that the work done in those old prewar days has been amply vindicated.
Let those who write ignorantly of the safe and easy life of the regular staff officer come and study this memorial, and remember that this is not the full tale of officers who held staff appointments and gave their lives in the war-
And so on. Whatever the minister has in mind regarding any reduction in the staff, I do hope that the country will not lose the services of those officers who made good in the war, who distinguished themselves, and who are now able to impart their knowledge to the generation that succeed them. I sincerely trust that other officers to come will have the privi-* lege of acquiring some of the knowledge and experience which these others have gained.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
There is an impression
in the House which I desire to correct to some extent, namely, that these officers who are now in the permanent force are there of their own desire. To my knowledge a great many of the senior officers are men upon whom great pressure was brought to bear to remain in the service after the war. Most of the others were already in the permanent forces. By far the majority of both senior and junior officers retired and went back to their civilian occupations when the war was over. As one hon. member put it the other day, those officers returned to the plow, and returned gladly, and to-day they are doing their duty as citizens. But certain officers and noncommissioned officers who devoted themselves exclusively to the service before the war and won the seniority in the field, have remained in the service under pressure, brought to bear by the Department of Militia when the war was over. Those are the men, I think, whom the country wants to see retained, the men who know, and those are the men who, if we are ever again faced with war, will be responsible for organizing our military force on a basis which will enable it to be administered efficiently, and so save the lives of thousands of men who might otherwise be sacrificed. Had Canada been equipped with the officers who to-day are in the Militia Department, I have no hesitation whatever in saying that thousands of our soldiers would not have been sacrificed as they were. The same condition applied to the British army and to every other army in the late war. Has it ever occurred to hon. members why Germany was able to withstand the onslaught of so many other nations? Mr. Chairman, it was because at the outset she had the benefit of a thoroughly trained and organized army. If we cast aside the men who have the knowledge and the training, we are, so to speak, cutting our own throats, and if another war should occur the absence of these trained men may mean the sacrifice of our sons to no purpose.
Subsection 5 of section 5 agreed to.
On subsection 6-provision for retirement, etc.:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
If economies are to be effected it is possible that the services of some of the minor officers may have to be dispensed with on account of the work being diminished. Such a case as this might arise: an officer at the time his services were dispensed with might be

National Defence
*within one year of the conclusion of the term which would entitle him to a pension. Under this subsection I want to make it possible for him to qualify for his pension.
I have been considering it for the last day or two, and I think we would be sufficiently generous if we changed the three years to two.
In reply to my hon. friend in reference to the gentlemen he has named, I fully agree with everything that he has said regarding their qualifications both as gentlemen and officers. I do not like to discuss in Parliament the names of such distinguished men. I might say, however, that Sir Henry Burstall had attained the highest position possible in the militia, what we call the blue ribbon-he had become Inspector General. I think I was not ungenerous in my recommendation, for he was entitled to a pension. I repeat, I do not like to discuss these gentlemen in public, because certainly it is no fault of theirs in the way of lack of qualification cr ability that they are being retired. The record of Sir Henry Burstall and of General Gwatkin is well known to all of us and will bear comparison with the record of the most distinguished military men in any country.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I think there is a serious principle involved in this clause. Having been a member of the Pensions Committee of this House fur two years past, if this clause carries I do not see why the returned soldiers should not ask that their disabilities be considered, although they occur two years after their discharge from service. I think you are establishing a very dangerous precedent in passing this clause, and so far as I am personally concerned I do not think it is wise to entertain it. I am again a member of that committee this year, and I feel that the idea of adding two or three years to the length of service in order to grant a man a pension is absolutely unsound. I know of many cases of real hardship under the provision of our Pensions Act, that if a soldier's disability occurs after a certain limited time after his discharge he is not entitled to a pension. But if this consideration is to be extended to the men affected1 by this bill, I think the Pensions Committee will approach their duties next week with a very different idea as to what is just and right in regard to pensions for disabled men.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is in error and is apparently confusing entirely
different classes of pensions. This has nothing to do with the Pension Board.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I understand that. This is a Civil Service pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: There are several acts involved in this clause, but it does not give a pension to any person-

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It is not a disability pension at all.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It does not give a pension to any person who is not entitled to one; but it does put us in a position to deal a little more generously with officers or civil servants who have to be retired. It does not deal with pensions for disability due to war service; it applies to another act altogether.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I thoroughly understand that, but I cannot help thinking that the minister is confusing the point. This man would not be entitled to a pension unless he had one, two or three years' more service than he actually had to his credit at the time of his retirement. Therefore by giving the Governor in Council authority to add from one to three years to this man's service he is entitled to a pension which he would not otherwise be qualified for. I understand that it is not a disability pension, -but a civil service pension. I have no great quarrel with civil service pensions, although there is a considerable body of opinion that holds the principle to be rather unjust, for people in all walks of life do not get pensions when they become too old to work. * Personally, I think civil servants should be paid salaries sufficient to enable them to accumulate enough during their official life to provide for their old age. If they are to be given a pension, I think they should contribute as those do who receive the benefit, for instance, of an old age pension fund.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Of course, other pension acts are involved here-what is known as the Calder Act, and any other Civil Service pension law that may be in force. But under the Military Pensions Act the contributions of the members of the permanent force made the fund absolutely self-sustaining. That condition, of course, could not prevail during the war, when the casualties became increased beyond anything we had ever experienced.
National Defence

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That puts a different aspect on it. I had understood that the Government contributed large sums toward these civil service pensions.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
This is a military
service pension, not a civil service pension.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I still contend, however, that this clause is unsound. I am sure that hon. members have been disappointed in the minister's civil government estimates, as, indeed they have been with nearly all civil government estimates so far brought down. The Finance Minister made it plain the other day that the Government had not said they would practise economy this year. I was a little disappointed in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Oh, no; I did not say
that.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Well, that they had
not made any statement with regard to economy; I do not want to misquote the minister. We certainly expected a saving in the Militia Department by the co-ordination of these different arms of the service. We all feel that in the years to come, expenditure for military purposes should be reduced, and I see no reason for increased expenditure now under the head of civil government in connection with the administration of this branch of the service. I do not approve of this clause, and I do not think it should carry.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I move that subsection
6 be amended by striking out the word "three" in line 26 and substituting therefor the word "two."

On section 6-regulations:

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
What is the meaning
of the words "such regulations as are deemed necessary or advisable?" Would not "necessary" be sufficient?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (East Kootenay, Minister of Public Works) :
subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
When these estimates were under discussion on Tuesday evening last, there was a desire expressed by some of the members of the committee for a fuller explanation with regard to the transfer of certain employees from the
5 p.m. engineering branch, outside service, to other branches of the service. At that time I stated that these officials were not permanent officials, had not been classified and admitted into the service as permanent employees, and that being temporaries, they would naturally come under the contingencies vote. I find that that statement is confirmed by a letter written in October of last year, when the chief accountant advised the Auditor General that it would be necessary on account of these transfers being of temporary officials to have them put under the contingencies vote instead of the outside vote. I think that explains the situation satisfactorily. It was also suggested that I should give the committee the total expenditure last year under the civil government vote. I find that the expenditure last year amounted to $557,545.52. It was also suggested that I should explain the item at the bottom of page 96 of the Estimates, "To provide for new appointments if required, $5,000." That item is to provide for unforeseen expenditures. It may become necessary to make one or two new appointments this year, and it is for that reason this item has been put in.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
Should that really not be counted as a contingency? Is it customary-as far as my knowledge goes it is not-to put an item under details of civil government such as appears at the bottom of page 96, " To provide for new appointments if required, $5,000 "? Mr. HOCIfEN: The minister gives two contradictory reasons for making these increases. He first increases a man because he is inefficient or has reached an age when he ought to retire. He has increased the salary of the librarian because he is going to retire, and I presume if he were an efficient officer he would be retained. Then the minister increases the salary of another officer on the ground of efficiency. I would point out that if the House adopts this increase, next year you will have to pay the Deputy Minister of Public Works $10,000, and that will carry from him to the Deputy Minister of the Interior and the Deputy Minister of Railways, and so on to all the other departments.
It will be observed that the deputy ministers' salaries have been fixed generally at $6,000. Now you fix one of them at $10,000, and naturally and inevitably every deputy minister will want to be placed on a par with that increase-he will feel he has a right to it. I doubt very much whether the Deputy Minister of Finance has any heavier responsibilities than the Deputy Minister of Public Works. The Public Works Department requires a permanent head with a great deal of experience and ability and, sometimes, resistance, and so far as the actual work and worries of office are concerned I think the Deputy Minister of Public Works should get more salary-if there is going to be any difference at all-than the Deputy Minister of Finance.
My argument is this, Mr. Chairman, we fixed $6,000 as the salary of deputy ministers; that was an increase of $1,000 on the old scale. Now, that strikes me as being a pretty good salary. We will say that these men are capable and efficient; I believe they are. But the $6,000 that they earn is as much remuneration as they could command in private employment if you take into account that when they retire from the public service they get a retiring allowance. Let a man go into private employment at a salary of $8,000, or possibly $10,000-a substantial increase, it may be said, upon the government scale; but it must be remembered that when the private employee ceases to be able to work he has to fall back upon his own reserves, while a man occupying the position of a deputy minister falls back upon the pension list and continues to live at the expense of the country when he retires. I submit therefore that if you 
take that into account and a good many other things also, a deputy minister is much better off. For instance, a man in private employment has to make good in everything-he has to show results or he loses his job. On the contrary, a man in the public service is not required to make good in the same way, and that is an important consideration when you are fixing salaries. Take that into account as well as his pension, his short hours of work, and all the other advantages and perquisites of his office, and I submit that $6,000 is good pay for a deputy minister.
These deputies were satisfied to accept $5,000 until a couple of sessions ago, when the salary was raised to $6,000. This looks to me, Mr. Chairman, like the beginning of an agitation within the service to boost the salaries of deputy ministers, and they have selected my hon. friend's department as the place of attack.
I would warn the House that if this increase is granted we may expect every session to be met with demands from deputy ministers for a similar increase.
It does not seem to me that this is the time to add $4,000 to the salary of a public official. If $6,000 was enough during 1921, it is surely enough now, and it is going to be worth a good deal more as time goes on. Conditions are stabilizing in this country-they must if we are going to carry on-the cost of living is coming down, but the rate of salaries is going up, and not going up by small increases, but by chunks of $4,000.
I think this proposition is simply out- [DOT] rageous, and I am surprised that my hon. friend, who has preached economy so effectively all through the country, should be the first to propose a sixty-six per cent increase to one official in his department, knowing as he must, with his long experience in this House, that every deputy minister will be clamouring for similar treatment. I am sure he is putting upon his colleagues a load of responsibility from which they should shrink, and which should have led them to say to him: " No we won't make this increase this year." I submit that this $4,000 should be struck out. I notice all the way down that there are increases. I presume that these other increases are made in accordance with the Civil Service rates, and are statutory-I do not know whether I am right or not-but certainly we should not add four-sixths to the salary of one official

Certainly there never should be defalcations, and the late government did everything it could to discover just what they were and to punish the defaulters. But I am not taking that into consideration, nor was my hon. friend when he was considering salaries. Another time perhaps we might say something further about that matter, but this is not an appropriate occasion.
As I say, the average salary of that department amounts to only $1,124 a year. Now there is a slight increase in numbers, so it cannot be said that we had too many employees there. As to the duties of the office, I do not think that hon. members really appreciate the weight of responsibility that does rest upon the officials of that office. At one time the finances of the country were of a very different character to what they are to-day. To look after the national debt alone imposes a tremendous responsibility upon the Deputy Minister of Finance. What the minister has said in connection with the difficulty of keeping men in that position who can do the work is perfectly true. I know what the troubles have been in the past, and I appreciate my hon. friend's troubles now. I am convinced that the work is cheaply paid for at $10,000 a year. I endorse very thoroughly what
my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) said, that this vote ought not to be made use of for the purpose of increasing other salaries generally. I would like to ask the minister whether or not the auditors who have been going through the department are proceeding with their work and whether it is his hope, as it was mine, that we shall be able to get as a result of this examination such a system of preaudit as will make impossible any further defalcations. We have to-day accountants and book-keepers in every department. My idea is that that is an entirely unnecessary expense; we ought to have everything of this kind brought into the Finance Department. subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
How is this medical inspection carried out? It seems to me that some of the present regulations dealing with the inspection of immigrants on the other side of the Atlantic are decidely obnoxious. I am advised that this medical inspection is conducted in a most unscientific and unsanitary manner. An old friend of mine coming across not very long ago told me that not only the immigrants but the saloon passengers boarding the ship at Liverpool were subjected to unheard-of indignities, an officer using his fingers to manipulate the eyelids of each passenger, without cleansing his hands between each operation. It did not matter what any of these passengers were suffering from, whether barber's itch, cancer or granulated
eyelids, it was all the same to this officer, and as a result of the rough and unsanitary method adopted one lady suffered very severely with her eyes all the way over.
I believe in thorough inspection of immigrants, but surely it can be done in a scientific and humane manner. But apparently the Liverpool treatment is mild compared with what takes place on this side. At .the port of landing here is where the real embargo begins-a kind of slaught-ered-on-the-dock, as it were. It is a shameful thing for this nation that men and women of all classes are herded together in pens waiting for inspection. I think that state of affairs should be altered at once.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
I am going to give the House the type of advertising that was circulated in the States some years ago to attract immigrants to this country, because I hope that future advertising will not be along the same lines. Referring to the western provinces, where settlers were invited to take up land, the advertisement ran something like this:
It was a common thing up there for the farmers to grow from forty to fifty bushels of Number One wheat to the acre. What one man can do, another can do. Those farmers up there have more real money to spend than any other people on the American continent.
We have been wondering why people attracted to this country by such immigration pamphlets do not remain here. Is it surprising that immigrants become disgusted, and leave when this sort of pamphlet entices them to pick up gold bricks, and instead they find a lot of hard work. I hope that this is not the sort of advertisement that is going to be circulated in future, unless we want to lose most of the immigrants who are attracted to this country by such misrepresentation.

I would like to add to what has been stated by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) in regard to medical inspection on the other side of the Atlantic. I have a case on my hands now of a Scotch family, the members of which bought their tickets and checked their baggage about a year ago. After they had gone through the preliminaries and were ready to sail, a doctor stopped one of the children, a little, girl, on the ground that she was mentally deficient. These people had sold all their goods in order to put themselves in funds for the voyage, and as a result of the doctor's action they had to postpone their voyage, and go to work, boarding out all the time. After a year the doctor finally passed

speechtext:
I understand she came on some time before the deputy was ap-

pointed. As regards the Department of Immigration, I would like to make one comment in view of certain observations that have been made. Up to the war our immigration had increased almost continuously. It was at its highest point just before the war-some 448,000 in one year. The population undoubtedly was increasing-not, of course, at the full speed of the immigration returns and of the natural increase as well, but, proportionate to that, the increase was equal to that of any other country. The United States itself has a tremendous immigration. Every country in the world has immigration. It is true, as my hon. friend (Mr. Manion) says, that the immigration into Germany was the least marked of all, particularly subsequent to 1878. But every country, particularly every northern country, has immigration. Our immigration figures are most satisfactory up to 1914. Naturally the war practically put a stop to immigration; everybody knows the reason why. With the cessation of hostilities the Department of Immigration was reorganized to meet the situation. The returns for last year show results; the returns for this year, I have not the slightest doubt, will show good results as well. Indeed, we might have had hundreds of thousands more immigrants-and no one knows this better than the minister himself-had we opened the doors and let them in. But the laws of this country, and the will of the people reflected in those laws, are such that we do not propose to open the doors indiscriminately to immigration. A great deal of the expense, a great deal of the executive activities of the department, are directed to the selecting of immigration, the weeding out, at the proper point for doing so of those who come. I should be sorry indeed to see anything in the way of slackening of energy on the part of the Immigration Department. Certainly there is work enough there for a good deputy; the bigger and the abler the deputy, the better results we are going to have. If there is any department of government in which I would like to see increased rather than diminished activity, it is the Department of Immigration and Colonization. Furthermore, in western Canada at the present time, as all of us know, there is a great voluntary movement, a big voluntary organization, which is interesting itself in colonization. I have not myself gone fully into the details of its organization, but I know many of those who have put them-

Stipply-Immigration
selves behind it and are determined to make it succeed. That organization should have close relations with the Department of Immigration and Colonization, and the work of the two together should, I think, go a long way to solve the problem of peopling the near-railway lands of western Canada. The time now is not to talk about slackening down the activities of the Immigration Department, but rather to speed them up. We are sufficiently past the war to get the impetus we need so much in this country. The nation that is going to succeed best in the post war period is the nation that directs its immigration policy along soundest lines and puts the most horse power and momentum behind it.

Mr. Chairman, I did not have the slightest idea of saying anything in regard to these estimates, but I wish to support as strongly as I can the remarks that have just been made by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). If ever there was an occasion for liberality in connection with our immigration policy, it is the present. It is only a year or two since, under the influence, I presume, of the leader of the Opposition, something like $500,000 was appropriated by the government to carry out surveys and plans for the redemption of southern Alberta through the irrigation projects that have been set on foot in that province. I want to give the hon. leader of the Opposition credit for hard work and painstaking effort in connection with these projects. Now, what is our position to-day? I am not going to depend too much upon my memory to-night, because I did not expect to speak on this subject. But of the 12,000,000 acres to the south of Calgary that are within the boundaries of the area affected by the drought, 5,000,000 acres approximately are in the hands of farmers. In that area there are 20,000 farmers, or, allowing four to each family, a farm population of 80,000. With the help of the government they have started to lay out and extend their surveys to redeem that whole country from the affliction of drought. Let me point out to you what that means. Take Lethbridge as a centre, and draw a circle which will include the affected area. In 1915, the year of our bumper crop in that part of the country, we shipped from that area 41,000,000 bushels of grain. In 1916 we shipped
39,000,000 bushels. A dry season followed, and in 1917 the crop yield dropped to
about 18,000,000 bushels. The drought and the dry seasons continued, and in 1919 only 4,000,000 bushels were shipped from there.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
I will attempt, Mr. Chairman, to connect this up, if you will allow me to place a few figures before the committee. The area which in 1915 produced 41,000,000 bushels of grain for shipment, produced in 1919 only 4,000,000 bushels. In 1919 we shipped 4,000,000 bushels only, but 1920 was a better year, with more moisture, and our shipments rose to 19,000,000 bushels. Then last year again we had dry conditions and our shipments decreased to 7,000,000 bushels. So you will see how important a national problem it is when production drops down to almost one-tenth between the years 1915 and 1919. There is only one way to solve the problem and that is to place the farmers on a basis where they can depend upon sufficient production to make a living for themselves and their families, and the way to do that is to introduce artificial irrigation throughout that territory. That is what we are doing. Those farmers have bonded their farms for that purpose to the amount of $40 per acre.
Now the application my remarks have to the item under discussion is simply this: This is a question of colonization. The individual farms out there are large in area, and the farmers, in order to make a success of irrigation, must subdivide their farms into plots not exceeding 160 acres each, and engage in a more intensified agriculture. For that purpose immigrants have to be found and brought into this country who are acquainted with irrigation methods. That must be done through the Department of Immigration, and the department must have sufficient funds available and enough men at its disposal to go out into the irrigation districts of the United States and carefully select immigrants who have had experience in irrigation methods. Every town and every city in southern Alberta is interested in this question; our railroads depend upon it, and I trust that when the minister brings down his final estimates they will contain an appropriation to help fill up that southern Alberta country with a suitable class of immigrants who will help subdivide these lands and bring up their families on them.

In 1921 we col-9 p.m. lected in round figures, $209,000,000 at a cost of $5,000,000. As my hon. friend knows, these estimates cover both Customs and Excise. I would point out that although in item 13 on page 8 there is an apparent increase of $10,745, that is [Mr. Jeliff.l
really a sub-normal increase. The normal increase would 'be about double) that amount. We have 231 clerks in the service who are entitled to statutory increases, and if conditions were normal the salaries of last year would be increased this year by $17,945. Now, there is an increase of $10,000 which I may explain. Some hon. gentleman referred to a remark which had dropped from the lips of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) that when a new minister came in he wanted a staff. I think it is only right he should have one, and when I was on the other side of the House I always advocated that, not only should a minister have a staff of his own, who should follow his fate, and when the minister goes out should go out with him, but that the members of the House are entitled to secretaries of their own. I do not think it is right that we should send our private papers down to a room where there are 50, or 60, or perhaps 100 stenographers, and where the papers would be open to the curiosity of all-comers. But this increase of $10,000 is due to the fact that we have taken advantage of a clause of the Civil Service Act, which provides that in any case where the commission decides that it is not practicable, in the public interest, to apply this act to any position or positions, the commission may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, exclude such position or positions in whole or in part from the operation of the act. Under that recommendation, the commission have excluded certain positions; for instance private secretary, secretary-clerk as they call him, and the secretary to the executive, one senior clerk-stenographer, one clerk-stenographer and one confidential messenger. That accounts for the increase. As I said, if things were as usual, we would have the ordinary amount of salaries, plus the statutory increase of $17,945, but this increase, with the $14,160, will make a total of $32,105. The salaries of nine positions, amounting to $12,630, have been discontinued during the past year, and a reduction of $8,730 has been effected by promotion, transfer, etc., making a total saving of $21,360, or a net increase of $10,745. I may say that the positions to which the minister was allowed to make appointments in his department are those which I have enumerated, secretary clerk, $3,360; secretary to the executive, $1,860; senior clerk-stenographer, $1,630, clerk-stenographer, $1,260, and confidential messenger. So that this is not an increase, it is a subnormal increase.
