I do not think the House is desirous of merely having taxes imposed. The imposition of taxes would not pay our debt very fast; we have to collect the taxes. The collection is the important part, and to collect the taxes, we must have a staff to do the work. The staff has been found insufficient to do the work properly. As I said a few minutes ago, the outside work comes inside. The commissioner and the assistant commissioner are not able to cope with the work which is imposed upon them. The minister himself is not able to attend tc all the work of receiving delegations from morning till night. This takes another officer whom we are going to call General Executive Assistant, who is going to be an assistant to all these officers in the department. For this position a man is required who knows thoroughly the customs laws, the excise law, all the regulations that are passed by the department, who is familiar with seizures, with all the routine of the department, who knows the interpretation to be given to the various items of the tariff, the various regulations that are being passed, who can assist the minister to receive delegations, and who can be a supervisor of all the work done in the department and be in a position, by his knowledge and experience, to control it. This is an absolute necessity; otherwise,
the officers at present in the department could not cope with the work.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: A little further down the list I notice a supervisor of refund claims and further on four checkers. Will the minister explain just what are the duties of supervisor of refund claims?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Those are refunds of overpaid duties. All those claims for refunds, after they have passed through the hands of customs officer at the port, come to the department, and they have to be checked and controlled. This supervisor certifies all claims that are made and the moneys paid back for refunds.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
Do I
understand that those are corrections that have been made by officers of the department? In other words, are they mistakes that must be corrected?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Yes, very often a man will import some goods, and they turn out to be not according to the order. In that case, if, within the time allowed by law, be returns the goods, he is entitled to a refund, because he does not use them. There may be errors in the invoice or in the appraisal. Sometimes, machinery that comes to this country does not suit the purpose for which it was ordered. It is returned, and it would not be fair to keep the money collected as duty upon such goods. We refund the money to the importers. I understand that the money saved pays the salary of the officer in charge, and the staff as well, ten times over.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Does the refund include the moneys that are paid back to certain manufacturers when gnods are exported?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: The manufacturers are given a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty on raw materials entering into the manufacture of goods that they export.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: The minister says that the important thing is to collect the revenue. I would suggest that the really important thing is to retain the revenue, and not pay some $15,000,000 back to the manufacturers in the form of a drawback. What percentage of the duty, is paid in the shape of drawback, and on what articles?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: It would be difficult to answer that question ih detail offhand.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
Does the minister think that it is good business to pay $10,000 for handling $15,000,000 in the way of draw-

Supply-Customs and Excise
back? My hon. friends to the right contend that we should have a tariff in order to get a revenue. Well, is it a sane policy to -pay $15,000,000 in the form of a drawback on raw material when our own natural resources are undeveloped?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: A rebate of 99 per cent of the duty on raw materials entering into the manufacture of articles that are exported is allowed. The manufacturing of these goods provides labour in Canada, and we desire to encourage our export trade. We lose nothing. We did not 'have the raw material, but we had the benefit of the labour, and we keep one per cent of the duty to pay expenses.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I would ask the question put by the ex-Minister of Finance so persistently in -the Tariff Commission: Where do you get your revenue?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: We get it from the articles that are imported and remain in Canada for consumption. We get our revenue from the excise and income taxes and the -sales tax. That is where we get our revenue; but we want to encourage Canadian industry.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: If foreign material is required for the manufacture of goods in Canada we tell the manufacturer to bring in that material and pay the -duty, and when he exports the goods we will refund 99 per cent, keeping one per cent for the trouble of putting through the entry.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
I want to draw a point
to the attention of -the minister and also to the notice of my hon. friends to the right, who appear to be getting a great deal of satisfaction out of his remarks. We import steel and iron from the United States for the manufacture of agricultural implements. On that material we pay a duty. The Canadian manufacturer makes the implements and if he sells them in Canada the cost to the Canadian consumer is increased by the extent of that duty. I think my hon. friend will agree in that statement. If, however, the manufacturer exports those implements to the United States he gets a drawback on the duty. So that the actual fact of the matter is that our Canadian manufacturers are thereby enabled to supply the American farmer with Canadian implements cheaper than the Canadian farmer can obtain them in Canada. Does the minister think that that is a desirable policy?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Rolled steel and pig iron when used in the manufacture of mowing-machines, reapers, harvesters, binders, and attachments for binders get a drawback of 99 per cent. The American does not enjoy the advantage of making the implements, and I do not think that Canadian implements, by reason of the drawback, sell cheaper in the United States than in Canada.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
I am glad to have even
one solitary voice in support of my remarks. My hon. friend says that these implements would be cheaper in the United States than in Canada. I am not able to go into that question now, because I do not know the price of agricultural implements in the United States, but it has been the practice to pay this drawback and it is intended to encourage manufacturing on this side of the line. If you have to import raw material it is only fair that when you do not consume the finished product here you should get a rebate upon it. We do not lose anything because our workmen are employed.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
What are the chief
articles on which this drawback is paid?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: There are various kinds of raw material on which the drawback is paid, but I cannot name them offhand. If the hon. member will put a question on the Order Paper I will see that he gets the information.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Does the minister think that one per cent pays the full expense in connection with this matter?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I am informed, not.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
I was thinking that if
it did, and you could run the whole department as cheaply as that, you could save money.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
Is it not
a fact that a drawback is paid on the duty on raw materials that go into the manufacture of implements sold in Canada?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
In the Customs Tariff
Act, at page 96, under the heading "Goods subject to drawback for home consumption" in article, No. 1002, there is a list of articles on which a drawback is given.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
That provision was
made at the time of the last reduction in duties on these articles. Is it not a fact that by means of the rebate or drawback as it is called on the raw material, the export trade thus developed adds to the scale of

Supply-Customs and Excise
production that it brings down the cost of the manufactured article in the home country?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
Why is it that we do not
use our raw materials in the manufacture of these goods? Since we are told that we should develop our natural resources, why do we import such raw material as iron and steel and other things that enter into the manufacture of implements to-day when our own forests and mines abound in these things and 250,000 men are idle at home? Is this the policy that we are going to maintain as a national policy?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I asked a question a little time ago, but I did not get an answer from you, nor from the minister, and I rather think he treated it as a joke. I should like to know now, through the chairman, if remarks regarding export liquor houses in dry provinces are in order?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: That matter will come up later, Mr. Chairman, when the outside service is discussed. I did not treat the question as a joke. It is a very serious question and I am ready to discuss it with my hon. friend when the other estimates come up.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I understood that point to be well covered by your ruling, Mr. Chairman, on the first day that estimates were submitted. You then ruled that the general policy of the department, whether directly or indirectly connected with the item before the committee, might be discussed within reasonable limits. Therefore with that ruling in effect it is perfectly clear that the hon. member is in order in discussing the outside service.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: What is the question?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
The province voted "dry" by a very large majority, and yet there are export liquor houses in operation that can not be controlled by the provincial government, and up to the present time the federal government has refused to take action for their suppression. Those houses serve as supply depots for the bootlegger, and also for those who are running liquor across the line into the United States, cars going backwards and forwards at all hours of the night. The work of the police who are kept there in an effort to control the situation leads sometimes to danger to life, because these liquor runners are armed and desperate men. What is the attitude of
the minister towards these export liquor houses?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I do not think they are under our jurisdiction, Mr. Chairman, because they are duty-paid liquor stores, and the moment we get our duty we have no more control over them. If my hon. friend means there are any bonded warehouses, my reply is that we do not grant any licenses for them unless we have the consent of the attorney general in the province. There are only two bonded warehouses in Saskatchewan, the licenses for which were granted long ago. I think my hon. friend is dealing with a matter which comes more under the jurisdiction of the provincial government than of this Government.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: There are more than two. I think I am using the proper term, "export liquor houses."

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: They are not bonded warehouse's.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I have received several petitions from local people protesting against those export liquor houses. The Minister of Agriculture was, I believe, in the provincial house when this controversy took place. The provincial government has always taken the attitude that it has gone as far as it possibly could in barring those houses.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: It is not a matter within our jurisdiction.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: The question has been discussed many times as to who is responsible, and we are led by the provincial authorities to believe that the federal government is responsible.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. They are not bonded warehouses, they are duty-paid warehouses, and entirely under the control of the provincial government. I am informed that there are only two bonded warehouses in Saskatchewan, and that the licenses for those were granted quite a while ago. I am also informed that the licensees have only been granted sufficient time to liquidate their stock, and have no right to import any more liquor.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I am told there are seventeen such houses.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that the licenses were granted under the approval of the attorney general of the province?

Supply-Customs and Excise

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: That has been and still is the policy of the department. We do not grant any licenses unless we g'et the approval of the Attorney General attached to the petition for the license; at the same time we have the designation of the warehouse by him.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Perhaps I can throw a little light on the subject. The majority of the warehouses referred to by the hon. member for Qu'AppeMe (Mr. Millar) are in the electoral district of Assiniboia, and, along with 'him, I have received many petitions protesting against their continuance. Likewise, I personally know of some of the acts done because of these warehouses. I believe there are twelve or fifteen on the southern line in my own electoral district.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: They are not ours.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
Last year I placed questions on the Order Paper concerning those warehouses, and the replies given to me by the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue I accepted in good faith. Those replies were to the effect that the Dominion Government did not have any bonded warehouses there. Premier Martin took exception to that, and I believe he carried on a discussion with the then Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue, contending that the Dominion government was responsible, and repudiating the answers which had been given to me. When I returned home I complained that I had not been taken into the confidence of the premier of Saskatchewan and that in the provincial campaign he had used the information given to me by the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue.
As it appears to me the circumstances are these. On our referendum in Saskatchewan we voted for only a partially "dry" province, and not for a "bone dry" province. But it appears that certain liquor interests throughout Canada-and the charge is made that Jewish capitalists are at the back of it all-made application to the provincial government for the privilege of erecting warehouses in Saskatchewan. In my questions I used the word "license," but it seems that the authorities of Saskatchewan contended that I should have employed the word "tax." A tax of $1,000 was imposed for the privilege of erecting each of these liquor houses. I believe that at the last session of the legislature that tax was increased to $5,000. In correspondence and in discussion I have

taken the ground: If you want to carry out the wishes of the people of the province, as expressed in the referendum, why do you not impose a million dollar tax?
It seems to me that if the license had not been granted by the provincial govenrment the federal government would have had nothing whatever to do with the export business, because the buildings would not have been there. I protest in the name of decency and good government against those buildings being permitted, because the traffic carried on iby means of them is a menace to life and property and a disgrace and shame to the community. The women in those localities fear to remain alone because of the traffic that is being carried on by the rum-runners, desperate characters that come in all the way from as far south as Oklahoma in big cars, as many as eight such cars loaded with liquor leaving one small town in an afternoon. This is a condition that I object to, and I would be glad if something could be done to remedy it. For myself-and I am sure I speak also for my people-if it is a matter of the department losing revenue, I would rather see it go without one cent of revenue if the result would be to do away with the abuses to which I refer.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: The liquor to which my hon. friend refers is duty paid liquor, stored with the consent and on the responsibility of the provincial government. We did not get a cent of revenue from it. It was in the province before the law came into force. The moment the duty on it was paid, the liquor belonged to the individual and the Crown had no control over it. There are no bonded warehouses for export licensed by the Dominion government in Saskatchewan, with the exception of the two that I have just referred to. These two were licensed with the approval of the Attorney General of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
I would not like the
statement made by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), that the cost of Canadian goods to the Canadian consumer is increased by the duty, to pass wholly without challenge. There was a case not long ago in New Brunswick where it became necessary, through default under a contract, for the person entitled to certain goods to purchase them in the American rather than in the Canadian market. The result was that with practically the same freight mileage, the cost of a farm article of similar character delivered in New

Brunswick was higher than the Canadian cost by the amount of the duty, showing that the Canadian manufacturer did not take advantage of the duty. The statement of the hon. member for Marquette was, no doubt, made in good faith, but I think it was an attempt to sum up the prejudices of the party which he leads against the customs tariff of this country. It may have been based upon an observation made at some time or in some place under fortuitous circumstances, but in my judgment it is not a correct summing up of the general operation of the tariff. The round of applause with which he was greeted was not so much an expression of a concurrence in his view as it was a protest against the administration of a customs tariff.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: In answer to a question put, I think, by the hon. member for Marquette, did I understand the minister to say that the increase of $10,000 was due in part to his employing certain persons who would leave the department when he left?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Part of the increase is due to that.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Is that ordinary patronage?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: It is ordinary necessity, for the proper working of the minister's office.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
I do not think it is
ordinary necessity. I am opposed to the voting of $10,000 simply in order that a minister may have his staff leave when he goes. It is bad policy, because the efficiency they have acquired while under him is lost to the country. I am opposed to that kind of thing.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: The right hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Meighen) made the statement that the practice of paying drawback claims on raw material entering into the manufacture of implements sold in Canada commenced seven or eight years ago, at the time of the reduction of the duties on agricultural implements. Is that correct?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
I said I thought it took place on the occasion of the last reduction. But it may not have been at that time, for there was a reduction since-I think it was in the spring of 1919. I am not positive as to my information, but that is my impression.
Supply-Cicstoms and Excise

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I thought it was rather new light on this subject of the reduction of the duties on agricultural implements. The minister has in his department a tax-collecting organization, and within it there is another and smaller organization to hand back a portion of the taxes he collects. As has been suggested, the most important function of the taxcollecting agency is to retain the taxes collected. I submit that the minister should consider the advisability of adopting a saner policy in this regard and do away with the organization which has been set up within his department-not by him, of course-for the purpose of handing back a portion of the taxes taken in. He has a supervisor with assistants who receive salaries amounting to $8,000 for the purposes of these refunds. Would it not be better for the department simply to collect such taxes as they intend to keep?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: Can the minister give us any information as to the amounts refunded on duties collected on farm tractors under $1,400 in value? A rebate of these duties was authorized, I understand, in 1919. Some hon. gentlemen to our left have been criticizing the refund of duties, and I think it is important that the committee should know how much is refunded on tractors inported into Canada for farm purposes.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: All tractors valued at $1,400 and under were entered free of duty under the order of remission and refund. There was no refund, because they were entered free.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: How is it that Canadian manufacturers are importing steel and iron from the United States or elsewhere when we have down in Nova Scotia a steel industry whose workmen are employed only on half time? Is that encouraging home industry?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: That is a matter I would have to consult the manufacturers about. It is more related to their business than to the administration of this department.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
With regard to the remark of the hon. gentleman for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter), he surely knew better than to make the statement he did that the duty does not enhance the cost of goods purchased in Canada. Does my hon. friend tell me that Henry Ford does not take advantage of the duty on automobiles \Vhen we are paying $260 more for a car on the Canadian side than on the American side?

Supply-Finance

I was also surprised to hear the ex-Minister of Finance say that farm machinery did not sell dearer in Canada than the United States, because when the Tariff Commission sat in New Brunswick last year I supplied the commission with a very comprehensive list setting forth the figures at which a certain firm was selling farm machinery in New Brunswick and in the state of Maine, at two points only six miles apart. The figures were very much higher for New Brunswick than the state of Maine. We paid as much as $65 more for a potato sprayer in New Brunswick than our neighbours paid for the same article in the state of Maine. This present year we are paying $9 per ton more than they are paying in [Maine for the same fertilizer shipped from a Canadian factory. I have the two price lists on my file upstairs, printed in a Canadian office, for fertilizer shipped from a Canadian factory. Going into the state of Maine, this fertilizer passes over two roads, and a longer haul, whereas it has only one road to pass over to reach the county of Carleton; yet it is selling for $9 more per ton in Carleton county than in the state of Maine. There is absolutely no manufacturing done at this fertilizer plant in Canada; they simply import the chemicals free of duty, mix the ingredients, barrel the fertilizer, ship it out, and sell it to the American consumer $9 per ton cheaper than to the New Brunswick consumer. Last year the difference in the price was $15 per ton; I have those price lists too on my file upstairs, on the company's own bill head, for this fertilizer shipped from a Canadian plant.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
Would the
minister say how much was expended under this vote last year?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: This is the first year of consolidation so it is pretty hard to tell, but I am informed that practically the whole salary list was paid, and that about $42,000 was expended under contingencies, with some bills still to come in.

speechtext:
I understood the
minister to say that the total revenue for excise and customs in 1921 was approximately $209,000,000 collected at a cost of approximately $5,000,000. How much of that was excise and how much customs revenue?

speechtext:
The customs revenue
for 1920-21 was $179,695,137.72 and excise $116,918,750.31.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: It will be noticed there is a small reduction in the offices of the Assistant Receivers General' and Country Savings Banks. This is due to some readjustment and the dropping of some temporary clerks.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: And the closing of one office I think.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
I think perhaps so.
There is an increase, apparently a large one, for printing, advertising, inspection, express and so forth. That is largely accounted for by the express charges on gold. As the House is aware, the export of gold from the Dominion by private parties is forbidden; the gold from our mines is received by the Government and 10 p.m. refined at the Mint. Then we have to express it to the United States, and the express charges on our shipments to the United States have increased very largely, but a gratifying feature of that increase is that it really represents a large increase in the output of our gold mines. For example, in 1918 our Canadian gold refined at the Mint was about 300,000 ounces; in 1919, 500,000 ounces; in 1920, 750,000 ounces, and in 1921, 1,100,000 ounces. All this passed through the Mint and had to be sent to the United States. That is the chief explanation of that increase.
There is a small increase for brokerage on the purchase of sinking funds, but that is governed entirely by the amount that may be purchased.
At the bottom of the list there is an increase of $100,000 for clerical assistance in connection with the transfer and registration of bonds, the flotation of loans, and so forth. The House is aware that we have to look forward to the issuing of very large refunding loans. That is the chief explanation for the very considerable increase in this item.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: With respect to the last item, I take it from what the minister says that this is to cover the cost of a refunding loan for the issue of $184,000,000 falling due in December. I take it that it is for the purpose of looking after a domestic loan that tnis money will be required.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
I think that is probably correct, although we have not yet made any final determination. It is, however, for refunding a domestic loan.

Supply-Finance

speechtext: The only reason I rose was to say that if it was for a foreign loan, accompanied with the usual underwriting, and the like, the increase seems unnecessary, but if it is for a domestic loan there is no doubt my hon. friend requires the vote.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
Would the minister
explain the item of $400,000 for printing Dominion notes?

amount as voted last year. It is the amount paid to the company which has the contract for printing our Dominion notes. There has been in that service of late years a considerable increase, explained simply by the volume of notes which the trade of the country requires.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: My hon. friend referred to the question of refunding loans. I think in one of the early discussions of the session reference was made to some financing in New York in regard to railway loans, and the remark was made, I think, by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) that he approved of that method of financing, because it avoided the payment of commission. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I contemplated at a later stage making a full explanation of that, but I have no objection to answer at once. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
With reference to this vote for the National Battlefields' Commission which has done good work, while there is no objection to this expenditure for maintenance of the national battlefield's park in the province of Quebec, I should like to ask the Government to consider the advisability of extending this work to other portions of Canada. I might refer to the ruined battlefields of the war of 1812 in the Niagara district. It would be a good thing for the people of Canada if something were done to commemorate and mark these battlefields. Those in the Niagara district are to-day in ruins and nobody knows who owns them. I hope the Government will take this matter up and do something. Then, there are the battlefields of the North West Rebellion, 1885, and also of the war of 1837. I hope this Government will consider this matter and extend these grants so as to include the various other battlefields in other parts of Canada which are in a neglected condition. I hope the Finance Minister will give the House some idea as to whether it is the intention of the Government to extend this work to the other battlefields of Canada. People from the United States who have visited the Niagara district have been much surprised that Canada is so far behind the times. If you go to Chattanooga in the southern states, and to the valley of the Cumberland, where Grant made his reputation in the war between the North and South, you will see how the United States people have remembered those who fought for their country, and have beautified the battlefields and have commemorated the deeds of the fallen.
I realize, of course, the financial situation and the high cost of money, labour and materials in these days, but I hope the Government will look into the matter with particular reference to the Niagara district.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS

I

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: The general object of these items, I think, ought to commend itself to the House. It is intended to assist the Canadian press in the distribution of news in a larger way than they could possibly do with their own resources. I think there is very strong reason why we should try to make the different sections of Canada better acquainted with one another. The press is not always wealthy. There is a long stretch of country between our eastern provinces and our western provinces which produces nothing in the way of revenue to the newspapers and it is, I think, largely for the purpose of bridging that long distance. At all events, it is not a source of any great wealth to the Canadian press. It helps them to give service which they otherwise would not give, and I think it is of the utmost importance that the various sections of Canada should be better informed of what is going on, each knowing the other section of Canada better than it does to-day. How far this is effected by the appropriation is a matter to be considered. I think the object of the appropriation is one which will readily commend itself to the House.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
There are, throughout the country, hundreds of worthy organ i*

Supp ly-Finance
zations that deserve grants if we had the money to subscribe to them; but in the financial position in which this country is now, I do not think we should increase three times the Government grant to this very worthy object. I am not complaining about the Boy Scouts; no doubt they do splendid work, but this does not seem to be the proper time for increasing the expenses of the country. We have given a grant of $5,000 to the Victorian Order of Nurses this year, and I think they received the same amount last year. I am not complaining about that. Someone says that they should have $10,000. I suppose if they had all the money we would like them to have, they might have $25,000 or $100,000. That is not the point. There are hundreds of worthy objects throughout the country, and that we should single out this worthy object for three times the grant of last year is something that I would like to protest against respectfully.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
Can my hon. friend
point to a more worthy object, one that has more far-reaching effects than the Boy Scouts Association?

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I do not know whether I am called upon or have a right to judge of the Boy Scouts as compared with hundreds of other worthy organizations. That is not the point. My hon. friend (Mr. Marler) has not quite grasped the point. I thought I had made it perfectly clear that this is an excellent institution. But until we meet, with ordinary revenue, the ordinary expenditure of this country, I, as a member of this House, and as representing the farming classes of the eastern townships, who are seeing their own revenues cut in half, am going to protest against any increase in the public expenditure of this country except for absolute necessities.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I accept my hon. friend's rebuke and, no doubt, the House does, in the same spirit.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I wish to go on record as most heartily supporting the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Me-Master) in opposing this $10,000 increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext:
The speech of the hon. member for Brome is so much in line with my thought on other questions that I have difficulty in dissenting from it. I am not going to break my heart if the committee does not want to increase this grant. It is for the committee to decide. There are
exceptions to all rules and if there is anything in which we are willing to make an exception, it would be in regard to the boys of the country who are going to be the men of to-morrow, the men who will be our successors at no distant date. I think this Boy Scout movement is a very commendable one; but I am not going to urge this inceased grant on the committee. If any hon. gentleman thinks this a grave departure from our sound policy of economy, he can divide the committee on the question; but I am not going to support him; I am going to have the liberty of voting against striking it out. I am not, however, going to urge this upon the committee at this late hour.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I am just as anxious for economy as any one in this House and will cut down the estimates wherever possible; but I have had some experience of the Boy Scout movement, and as I have no boys of my own, I am not speaking for myself in this case at least. There is no greater or more important work being carried on in Canada to-day than the Boy Scout movement. I have great respect for the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) but I do not think he has looked at this matter in all its bearings and in every phase in which we might Consider it. As has already been remarked to-night, the boys will be the men of to-morrow; they will take up the burden, and I hope they will carry the flag a great deal better than their fathers have done. No dollar that is spent is lost when it is spent in bettering the conditions of these same boys. I have much pleasure in supporting this appropriation at this particular time.

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE ADDRESS
speechtext: I have much pleasure in endorsing what the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) has just said regarding the Boy Scouts. I have a boy who is a Scout, and I do not think this money is thrown away. I think it is one of the best expenditures the country can make.
